text: {"answer": "Several trials and meta-analyses suggest intermittent fasting can produce weight loss comparable to or somewhat better than continuous calorie restriction. A randomized trial in obese women found that intermittent fasting combined with calorie restriction reduced body weight, fat mass and visceral fat, with a liquid-diet arm losing more weight [23334c40ad6b#0] [23334c40ad6b#1]. A high-protein intermittent-fasting, low-calorie diet also produced weight loss and improved arterial function in obese adults [c74e11d8769a#0]. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found intermittent energy restriction comparable to continuous restriction for weight loss and cardiometabolic outcomes [e5aee0e45fc5#0] [ebc373b389d7#0]. Harvard's Nutrition Source notes that one randomized trial of 100 obese individuals over a year found intermittent fasting no more effective than daily calorie restriction [44e3472ec92d#7]. A Cochrane review of 22 trials reported by ScienceDaily found no significantly greater weight loss than standard diet advice [5a896703f2e3#0]. Overall, the evidence indicates intermittent fasting works mainly as a calorie-reduction method, with benefits similar to standard dieting rather than superior, and confidence is moderate given mixed and small trials.", "confidence": 62, "one_line": "Intermittent fasting produces weight loss similar to standard calorie restriction, though some reviews find it no better; evidence is mixed and moderate in quality."}
